name: Question 13
problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x(t))+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y(t)+1) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=1-{x}^{2}(t)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(y(t)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the behavior of the system's solutions near the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[1,\text{ }0]^{T}?$$\,$
The equilibrium is an 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}.
worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$f(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1) \\ 1-{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1))=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1))=\frac{1}{y+1} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1))=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1-{x}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1))=-\frac{1}{y+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) & \frac{1}{y+1} \\ -2x & -\frac{1}{y+1}\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi ) & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 \\ -2 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )^{2}+2 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-1\pm \text{i}\sqrt{2}.$

Finally, since we have two complex eigenvalues with negative real parts, our equilibrium is an $\text{asymptotically stable}$ $\text{spiral sink}.$
